blog_summary: The blog post discusses the 'skyline operator' in database systems, which is crucial for multi-criteria decision-making applications. Adrian Colyer explains that the skyline operator returns objects that are not dominated by any other object in all dimensions. For example, in a hotels dataset with price and distance attributes, a hotel is in the skyline if no other hotel is both cheaper and closer to the beach. The paper introduces the Branch-and-Bound Skyline (BBS) algorithm, which efficiently computes the skyline using R-trees and nearest-neighbor search techniques. BBS is praised for its progressiveness, fairness, and I/O optimality, ensuring it only visits relevant nodes and avoids false hits or misses. The post also highlights incremental maintenance of skylines and variations like constrained skyline queries.
paper_title: Progressive skyline computation in database systems
paper_abstract: The skyline of a d-dimensional dataset contains the points that are not dominated by any other point on all dimensions. Skyline computation has recently received considerable attention in the database community, especially for progressive methods that can quickly return the initial results without reading the entire database. All the existing algorithms, however, have some serious shortcomings which limit their applicability in practice. In this paper we develop BBS (branch-andbound skyline), an algorithm based on nearest neighbor search, which is I/O optimal, i.e., it performs a single access only to those nodes that may contain skyline points. BBS is simple to implement and supports all types of progressive processing (e.g., user preferences, arbitrary dimensionality etc). Furthermore, we propose several interesting variations of skyline computation, and show how BBS can be applied for their efficient processing.
